subject: forensic-science
intro: Forensic science puts chemistry, biology and pattern evidence at the service of the courts, and it leads to work examining crime scenes, analysing evidence and explaining it under oath.

roles.title: Forensic Science Technicians
roles.what: Collect, identify, classify and analyse physical evidence from criminal investigations — testing weapons and substances such as fibre, hair and tissue — and may testify as expert witnesses, specialising in ballistics, fingerprinting or biochemistry.
roles.where: Crime-scene documentation and chain of custody from unit 2, pattern evidence, trace analysis and the DNA-profiling unit map one-to-one onto the laboratory disciplines of the job.

roles.title: Digital Forensics Analysts
roles.what: Investigate computer-based crimes: analyse digital evidence and security incidents, preserve and present computer-related evidence, and support criminal, fraud and law-enforcement investigations.
roles.where: The digital-forensics topic in unit 7 — evidence handling and examination — plus the Locard exchange principle and scientific-method foundations of unit 1 give you the investigative frame for cyber casework.

roles.title: Police Identification and Records Officers
roles.what: Collect evidence at crime scenes, classify and identify fingerprints, and photograph evidence for use in criminal and civil cases.
roles.where: Unit 2's scene search, sketching and photography and unit 3's fingerprints and bloodstain pattern analysis are the precise craft of evidence identification this role performs every shift.

roles.title: Detectives and Criminal Investigators
roles.what: Conduct investigations into suspected violations of federal, state and local laws to prevent or solve crimes, gathering evidence and building cases that can stand up in court.
roles.where: Knowing what the laboratory can prove — serology, DNA, trace and ballistics from units 3 to 7 — plus the admissibility and expert-testimony law of unit 8 makes an investigator a sharp consumer of science.
